assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Combustion
items.clue: The burning of a fuel in oxygen, releasing energy.

items.label: Soot (carbon particles)
items.clue: Solid particles of carbon released when a fuel burns in a limited supply of air.

items.label: Carbon monoxide
items.clue: A gas, formula CO, produced when a carbon-containing fuel burns in a limited supply of air so that the carbon is not fully oxidised.

items.label: Particulates
items.clue: Tiny solid particles suspended in the atmosphere, formed from solid particles such as soot and from unburned hydrocarbons released when fuels burn.

questions.stem: A monitoring station in a city records carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide and particulates in the air above a busy road. What do these three pollutants have in common?

options.text: All three are released when fuels are burned
All three form from nitrogen in the air
All three come from sulfur in the fuel
All three are gases like carbon monoxide

questions.explanation: The specification names the combustion of fuels as a major source of atmospheric pollutants, and all three of these are released when fuels burn.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes what most fuels, including coal, contain?

options.text: Carbon and/or hydrogen, and always a little sulfur
Carbon and/or hydrogen, and possibly some sulfur
Carbon and nitrogen, and possibly some sulfur
Sulfur and oxygen, and possibly some carbon

questions.explanation: This is what the specification states: most fuels, including coal, contain carbon and/or hydrogen and may also contain some sulfur.

questions.stem: A hydrocarbon fuel burns completely in a plentiful supply of air. Which two substances are released?

options.text: Carbon monoxide and water vapour
Sulfur dioxide and carbon dioxide
Carbon dioxide and water vapour
Carbon dioxide and hydrogen

questions.explanation: With plenty of air the carbon is fully oxidised to carbon dioxide and the hydrogen is oxidised to water, released as water vapour.

questions.stem: Solid particles and unburned hydrocarbons are released from a burning fuel. What do they form in the atmosphere?

options.text: A gas called carbon monoxide
Sulfur dioxide in the air
Carbon dioxide that causes acid rain
Particulates in the air

questions.explanation: The specification states that solid particles and unburned hydrocarbons form particulates in the atmosphere.

questions.stem: Petrol is burned inside a car engine and carbon monoxide is found in the exhaust gases. Why is carbon monoxide produced?

options.text: Nitrogen from the air combines with carbon atoms
The oxygen supply is limited, so combustion is incomplete
Sulfur in the petrol takes oxygen from the carbon
The oxygen supply is plentiful, so carbon burns fully

questions.explanation: Inside the engine the air supply is limited, so some carbon is only partly oxidised and carbon monoxide forms instead of carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Oxides of nitrogen are found in the exhaust gases of a hot car engine. Where does the nitrogen in them come from?

options.text: From nitrogen compounds present inside the fuel
From sulfur impurities reacting with hot air
From nitrogen in the air drawn into the engine
From nitrogen given off as the fuel breaks up

questions.explanation: Air is about four-fifths nitrogen, and at the high temperature inside the engine that nitrogen reacts with oxygen from the air.

questions.stem: A fuel contains carbon, hydrogen and a small amount of sulfur. It is burned in a plentiful supply of air. Which products are formed?

options.text: Carbon dioxide, hydrogen and sulfur dioxide
Carbon monoxide, water and sulfur dioxide
Carbon dioxide, soot and sulfur dioxide
Carbon dioxide, water and sulfur dioxide

questions.explanation: With plenty of air the carbon is oxidised to carbon dioxide, the hydrogen to water, and the sulfur impurity to sulfur dioxide.

questions.stem: A gas heater burns methane in a room where the air vent has been blocked, so the oxygen supply is poor. Which product now appears that would not be formed with plenty of air?

options.text: Carbon monoxide
Nitrogen dioxide
Unburned hydrogen
Sulfur dioxide gas

questions.explanation: With a limited oxygen supply the carbon in the methane is only partly oxidised, so carbon monoxide is formed instead of carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: A fuel burns with a smoky yellow flame in a limited supply of air and gives off black soot. Why is the soot produced?

options.text: The flame is so hot that it forces carbon out as solid particles
The sulfur in the fuel is left behind as solid soot
The fuel breaks apart into its elements, leaving solid carbon
Not enough oxygen is present to oxidise all the carbon, so some is released as solid particles
